The high-frequency scattering problems of electromagnetic fields scattered from electrically large scatterers are important and challenging.
The computational effort for the scattered field increases vastly with the growth of the electrical size of the considered scatterer.
The fast multilevel fast multipole algorithm (MLFMA) reduces the workload to O(N logN), but in the high-frequency regime, the computational workload is still too high to afford.
The GO method provides a fast way to calculate the reflected field from electrically large scatterers with frequency-independent workload.
The SBR method uses ray tracing, amplitude tracking, and physical optics to capture the scattered fields from complicated structures like cavities.
The GTD method calculates the diffracted fields from canonical wedge problems, but it breaks down near the shadow and reflection boundaries.
The UTD method uses the uniform asymptotic technique to overcome the breakdown problem of the GTD method near the transition regions.
The PO method approximates the induced current on the scatterer, leading to highly oscillatory integrals for the scattered fields.
The PTD method introduces an edge current to correct the PO current around the shadow boundary and in the deep shadow regions.
The ILDC technique calculates the diffracted wave fields by integrating the free-space dyadic Green's function and the uniform current over the surface of the scatterer.
The NSDP method can efficiently calculate the highly oscillatory wave fields from both the PO and ILDC techniques with frequency-independent computational workload and controllable accuracy.
The paper discusses high-frequency wave physics phenomena such as critical point contributions, Keller's cone, shadow and reflection boundaries, and creeping wave fields.

Other high-frequency methods and techniques mentioned in the paper include wave boundary element methods, rapidly oscillating quadratures, boundary integral methods, fast multipole method, and time-domain high-frequency methods.
The paper is an invited paper for the Commemorative Collection on the 150-Year Anniversary of Maxwell's Equations.
The paper was published in the Progress In Electromagnetics Research journal in 2016.
